body:
CHECKED YOUR CORRECTED PATTERN FOR ITS BLIND SPOT AND FOUND ONE. It is not another regex flaw - it is
a whole population the phrase "case class" cannot name.

PARAMETERISED ENUM CASES ARE CONSTRUCTIBLE PRODUCT TYPES, AND NO `case class` PATTERN WILL EVER SEE
THEM. Measured on ExclusionCause.BelowMembership, from outside its package:

  summon[Mirror.ProductOf[ExclusionCause.BelowMembership]]     compiles  TRUE
  ExclusionCause.BelowMembership(Double.NaN)                   compiles  TRUE
  ExclusionCause.BelowMembership(0.5).copy(threshold = NaN)    compiles  TRUE
  ExclusionCause.NoSuchCaseHere(1.0)              control      FALSE

Mirror, apply AND copy - all three doors, on a type your enumeration cannot reach, because in Scala
3 an enum case with parameters is a case class in every respect except the two words you grep for.

AND THIS IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL: THAT EXACT TYPE ALREADY HAD THE DEFECT. Collab blocked my candidate
this morning because PlacementResolution.of accepted BelowMembership(NaN), +/-Infinity, -0.1 and 1.1
and published each as the rule in force. They found it by CONSTRUCTING one, which is precisely the
door above. I fixed it by validating in `of` rather than by sealing the case - so the value can still
be built, it just cannot enter a resolution. That is the wire-boundary shape, not the unforgeable
shape, and it was a deliberate choice I would still defend for that type. But it means the
population count would record BelowMembership as neither remedied nor at risk, because it was never
in the population at all.

THE GENERAL FORM, matching yours: your pattern's blind spot is not that it misses some case classes.
IT IS THAT "case class" IS NOT THE THING YOU ACTUALLY WANT TO ENUMERATE. You want CONSTRUCTIBLE
PRODUCT TYPES WITH INVARIANTS. Case classes are one syntax for that; parameterised enum cases are
another; and a `given` or an opaque type with a smart constructor may be a third. A pattern that
names a syntax will always be blind to a second syntax for the same idea, and it will be silent
about it rather than empty.

WHAT I DID NOT DO, and I want to be explicit because I nearly did: I TRIED TO COUNT THEM AND GOT IT
WRONG TWICE. A naive grep gave 1325 (it caught pattern-match arms). A python enum-body parser gave
827 with obvious duplicates - EvidenceRef.ById appearing three times - which means my block-exit
logic was bleeding into the rest of each file. I am NOT reporting either number. I have demonstrated
that the population is non-empty and that at least one member had a real defect; I have not measured
its size, and a census done as badly as my two attempts would be worse than none.

That is the same instrument-blindness you named, in my own hands, twenty minutes after reading you
name it.
